prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part, B013, to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I have used the first-round exchange to test it on the chair's first question, whether the lattice clock is a distinct achievement. I think it is, and I can say what is new in measurement terms. The 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb, which made optical frequencies countable. The 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. A single ion gives superb accuracy but a low signal, so its stability averages down slowly. The lattice clock removed that limit through a different idea, Katori's: many neutral atoms held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, with the lattice light shift cancelled at the magic wavelength. Ye's group then showed what that buys: strontium clocks with fractional systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 and stability that lets clocks be compared in hours instead of weeks. The result has been reproduced and cross-checked in several independent laboratories, which I consider the strongest maturity evidence available to an experimentalist. It is already used for millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter searches. I would write the citation around the invention and realization of the lattice clock, not around an accuracy record or timekeeping in general, so that it reads as a distinct achievement and not as a continuation prize. On the chair's question about priority, the two steps are separable but I would credit them together: Katori's proposal and first demonstration of the scheme, and Ye's realization at the accuracy and stability frontier with the many-body clock. Crediting both under one citation also answers Olsson's concern, because the citation names the original idea and does not rest on the better-performing second group alone.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged in kind but I have narrowed it. A sceptic can still say this is a very successful step on a line the prize has honoured often, and that the largest scientific payoff, a redefined second and new-physics results from clock networks, has not yet arrived. Real contributions by Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Derevianko, Oates, Bloom and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups are left out of a two-name credit, and I have not verified early priority dates for the strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks to the standard I would want for a final vote. I also accept Pearce's point that broad support partly reflects a clean attribution and that the committee should not confuse that with scientific weight. The Higgs discovery has more weight, but I do not see a three-name attribution among four leaders of two large collaborations that I could defend, so the scientific merit of B013 has to be judged on its own terms, which I think it passes.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B013 first but says Ye already shared the 2005 prize, treats this as a possible reason to prefer B001 or B059, and notes that opening support may reflect clear attribution more than scientific weight.
responses.response: I want to correct the premise, because it carries weight in your fallback. The 2005 prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hänsch. Ye was a close collaborator of Hall in the comb work but was not a laureate, so the committee is not returning to a prior laureate and the same-laboratory-family concern is weaker than you state. The same error appears in several round-1 files (Eriksson, Johansson, Lindroth, Olsson as summarised by the chair) and I think we should all drop it. Your underlying point about weight versus attribution is fair. I would answer that the Higgs weight is real, but the 2013 prize already recognised the mechanism, and the committee cannot name three of four from ATLAS and CMS without an arbitrary cut. For IceCube I still hold that the diffuse flux is established while source identification is thin, so I would not put it ahead of the clock this year.

responses.point: Olsson worries that the prize should reward the original work and not the second group that did it better, and asks whether Katori and Ye are credited for one achievement or two separable contributions.
responses.response: I think this is the right test, and the citation can meet it. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and that is the invention. Ye's group is not merely a better second group: it showed that the many-atom scheme reaches 1e-18 with stability no single-ion clock matches, and that is what made the idea a measurement instrument. I would word the citation as 'invention and realization' so that both steps are named and neither is reduced to an accuracy record. If you find that Ye's contribution is mostly refinement of an existing scheme, tell me which result you would call derivative, because I have not found one that is. I also agree that we should not use the clock prize to settle a question about B015, where you have a declared interest, so I will leave B015 as a minor alternative and not argue it.

responses.point: Mehlig says the committee should rest the prize on what is new, many-atom interrogation with cancelled light shift and the 1e-18 regime, and not on the clock as a natural next step after 2005 and 2012, and he keeps B042 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree with the framing. Metrology precedent is an objection to answer, not an argument for the prize, and my first-round remark about the 2005 and 2012 prizes was meant as the objection. The new element is the combination of many atoms, a tight lattice and a cancelled light shift, which no comb or single-ion clock provides. On B042 I find the universality argument attractive, but you also report that it has almost no support here and that the credit problem is real, given Parisi's earlier prize and the exact solutions by others. I would not weigh it above B013 for that reason, and I do not think the committee's difficulty with it is a lack of respect for the physics.

responses.point: Lindroth states plainly that Katori's proposal and early demonstrations (2001 to 2003) and Ye's record-setting realization are the two decisive steps and that the other groups are secondary, while she ranks B009 low on diffuse credit.
responses.response: Thank you for stating the priority dates, and for the fuller record I will take them as the working position, though I cannot independently confirm every date. I still resist the word secondary for Lemonde and the SYRTE and PTB comparisons, since an accuracy claim is credible only when independent clocks agree. That argues for the citation wording and not for adding names. I also accept your and Pearce's objection to B009: Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth and Wrachtrup make a diffuse credit, so I am moving it out of my alternatives and putting B015 there instead, as a mature, instrument-driven result with a three-name trio.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock adds a distinct achievement beyond the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, as I argue, or still sees it as an increment.

I have not independently verified early priority dates for the strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks and rely on Lindroth's account. If a verified date showed that another group's contribution was equal in kind to Ye's, I would reconsider the pairing.

The redefinition of the second has not happened. I now think waiting is not justified, because the clock's measured performance is already delivered and reproduced, but I cannot rule out that a later year would give a stronger citation.
Whether the committee can agree on wording that credits the invention and the realization without reading as an accuracy-record prize.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B013: I have no Lund, mentor, company or collaboration tie to Katori or Ye. My former alternatives B009 and B037 sit close to my quantum optics and sensing interests. B037 remains an alternative, so I flag that proximity. My role in the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home at Chalmers, which bears on B054 and not on B013. I note that Johansson and Olsson have declared interests in B054 and B015 respectively, and I would treat their views on those candidates accordingly.
